'''Howard Levi''' (November 9, 1916 – September 11, 2002) was an American [[mathematician]] who worked mainly in [[algebra]] and [[Mathematics education|mathematical education]].<ref name="AMSN">[https://www.ams.org/notices/200306/inside.pdf ''Notices of the AMS'', June/July 2003, Volume 50, Number 6, p. 705.]</ref> Levi was very active during the educational reforms in the United States, having proposed several new courses to replace the traditional ones.

==Biography==
Levi was born in New York City in 1916.<ref name="AMSN" /> He earned a [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics from [[Columbia University]] in 1942 as a student of [[Joseph Fels Ritt]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=37383}}</ref> Soon after obtaining his degree, he became a researcher on the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name="fourcolor">[[Melvin Fitting]] – [http://comet.lehman.cuny.edu/fitting/fourcolor/fourcolor.html The Four Color Theorem] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150212093832/http://comet.lehman.cuny.edu/fitting/fourcolor/fourcolor.html |date=February 12, 2015 }}</ref><ref>For some details, consult: Mildred Goldberg – [http://www.gilderlehrman.org/collections/c66c2257-6a12-48d4-b345-482222175359 Personal recollections of Mildred Goldberg, secretary to the theoretical group, SAM Laboratories, The Manhattan Project; 1943-1946] ([[Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History]]).</ref>

At [[Wesleyan University]] he led a group that developed a course of geometry for high school students that treated [[Euclidean geometry]] as a special case of [[affine geometry]].<ref>{{cite book|author-first=Nathalie|author-last=Sinclair|authorlink=Nathalie Sinclair|title=The History of the Geometry Curriculum in the United States|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K7U6I3fxRSoC&pg=PA64|year=2008|publisher=IAP|isbn=978-1-59311-697-2|pages=64}}</ref><ref>Sitomer, H. – Coordinate geometry with an affine approach, Mathematics Teacher 57 (1964), 404–405.</ref> Much of the Wesleyan material was based on his book ''Foundations of Geometry and Trigonometry''.<ref>C. Ray Wylie, [http://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED085260.pdf An Affine Approach to Euclidean Geometry (p. 237 from the PDF document, p. 231 from the document itself)]</ref>

His book ''Polynomials, Power Series, and Calculus'', written to be a textbook for a first course in [[calculus]],<ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/2312681 Levi, Howard — An Experimental Course in Analysis for College Freshmen]</ref> presented an innovative approach, and received favorable reviews by [[Leonard Gillman]], who wrote "[...] this book, with its wealth of imaginative ideas, deserves to be better known."<ref>{{cite journal|author= Gillman, Leonard|authorlink=Leonard Gillman|title=An Axiomatic Approach to the Integral|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|year=1993|volume=100|issue=1|pages=16–25|url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/upload_library/22/Ford/Gillman16-25.pdf|doi=10.2307/2324809|jstor=2324809}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author= Gillman, Leonard|authorlink=Leonard Gillman|title=Review: ''Polynomials, Power Series, and Calculus'' by Howard Levi|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|year=1974|volume=81|issue=5|pages=532–533|jstor=2318616|doi=10.2307/2318616}}</ref>

[[Levi's reduction process]] is named after him.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Mead, D. G.|title=The Equation of Ramanujan-Nagell and [y<sup>2</sup>]|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|date=December 1973|volume=41|issue=2|pages=333–341|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1973-041-02/S0002-9939-1973-0327725-4/S0002-9939-1973-0327725-4.pdf|doi=10.2307/2039090|jstor=2039090}}</ref>

In his last years, he tried to find a proof of the [[four color theorem]] that did not rely on computers.<ref name="fourcolor" />

He died in New York City in 2002.<ref name="AMSN" />
